title-group.article-title: Methylprednisolone or dexamethasone? How should we choose to respond to COVID-19?: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

sec.title: Background:
sec.p: Methylprednisolone (MP) and dexamethasone (DXM) are commonly prescribed hormone drugs for treating coronavirus pandemic disease 2019 (COVID-19) patients, but conflicting results from previous studies and meta-analyses on their efficacy and safety necessitate further investigation. Therefore, in this study, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials to enhance the level of evidence and compare the efficacy and safety of MP and DXM in COVID-19 patients.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: We conducted a comprehensive search of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases to retrieve randomized clinical trials. Our primary outcome measure was all-cause mortality, with secondary outcomes including admission to the intensive care unit, length of hospital stay, mechanical ventilation, and adverse events.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: This study analyzed six randomized controlled trials involving 1403 patients (MP group: 704; DXM group: 699). The results of the analysis showed no significant differences in mortality rates, admission to intensive care units, hospitalization time, mechanical ventilation, or adverse events between the MP and DXM groups (P > .05). However, a significant difference was observed in the incidence of hyperglycemia between these 2 groups (RR = 1.78, 95% CI [1.09, 2.89], P = .02, I2 = 78%).

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: The results of this meta-analysis showed that there was no difference in mortality, ICU admission rate, hospital stay, mechanical ventilation, or adverse events between MP and DXM in the treatment of COVID-19. The incidence of hyperglycemia with methylprednisolone was higher than that with dexamethasone.
Keywords: COVID-19, dexamethasone, meta-analysis, methylprednisolone, randomized controlled trial
Received 2023 Apr 4; Received 2023 Jul 17; Accepted 2023 Jul 24; Collection date 2023 Sep 8.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: In December 2019, the emergence of the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)-induced coronavirus pandemic disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic posed an unprecedented threat to global public health.[1] It has been reported that 20% of COVID-19 patients eventually develop acute respiratory failure that necessitates critical care.[2–4] Respiratory and multi-organ failures were believed to be caused by severe cytokine and chemokine storms.[5] Consequently, patients with COVID-19 have been treated with immunosuppressive medications, such as corticosteroids.[6] However, corticosteroids’ role in COVID-19 treatment remains under discussion.[7]

Corticosteroids have become a popular therapeutic option for COVID-19 patients with hypoxia following the RECOVERY trial demonstration of a mortality benefit with low-dose dexamethasone (6 mg).[8] It is believed that corticosteroids can reduce the cytokine storm induced by IL-6. COVID-19 has been treated with methylprednisolone (MP) and dexamethasone (DXM),[9] but studies have varied on the superior efficacy between the two. Meta-analyses of 3 studies[10] found no significant difference between MP and DXM in terms of mortality or intubation. However, another meta-analysis of 5 studies[11] demonstrated that MP significantly reduced mortality and intubation compared to DXM. While both analyses had limitations, the authors were unable to draw definite conclusions from them. Data on the efficacy and safety of MP and DXM in treating COVID-19 remain unclear.[12]

Recent randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have demonstrated that methylprednisolone (MP) is more effective than dexamethasone (DXM) for the treatment of COVID-19.[13] However, due to uncertainties surrounding previous studies and meta-analyses,[10,14] a meta-analysis of RCTs was conducted to enhance the level of evidence and compare the efficacy and safety of MP versus DXM in COVID-19.

sec.title: 2.1. Search strategy
sec.p: The preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines were followed for conducting the current study.[15] A thorough search of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library from December 31, 2019, to March 13, 2023, turned up all relevant RCTs. The following search terms were used: “COVID-19” or “coronavirus” or “SARS-CoV-2” or “SARS-2” or “2019-nCoV” or “2019 novel coronavirus” and “Methylprednisolone” or “Medrol” or “Urbason” and “Dexamethasone” or “Desameton” or “Decaspray” or “Hexadrol.” The literature search strategies for each database are specified in Supplemental Digital Content (Table S1, http://links.lww.com/MD/J500). The language of searching for literature is limited to English only. In order to produce more thorough findings, the references were also manually searched. Two authors independently completed the work. All disputes were settled by a third investigator. The protocol for this systematic review was registered on INPLASY (INPLASY202330073) and is available in full on inplasy.com.

sec.title: 2.2. Inclusion and exclusion criteria
sec.p: Inclusion criteria: COVID-19 was diagnosed by chest X-ray or CT images, clinical symptoms, reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction, and a nasopharyngeal swab test. The positive patients were patients with COVID-19 over 18 years old. The treatment group used methylprednisolone, the control group used dexamethasone, and all the included studies were RCTs.

Exclusion criteria: review articles, conference abstracts, case reports, articles written in languages other than English, and research lacking the entire text or missing critical data were all removed.

sec.title: 2.3. Data extraction
sec.p: Two reviewers separately gathered information from the included studies. The third author discussed or settled any disagreements, if there were any. First author, publication year, study area, study design, inclusion standards, corticosteroid type, dose, and duration, control intervention, study outcome, and longest follow-up were all collected.

sec.title: 2.4. Outcome measures
sec.p: It just extracted and evaluated the cross-results involved in RCTs, omitting to extract the pertinent results of each study in the meta-analysis. All-cause mortality was the primary outcome measure, and admission to the intensive care unit, hospital stay time, mechanical ventilation, and adverse events were the secondary outcome measures.

sec.title: 2.5. Quality assessment
sec.p: Two writers independently assessed the quality of each study using the Revised Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for Randomised Trials (RoB 2).[16] It consisted of 5 domains, including the randomization process, deviations from the intended intervention, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, selection of reported outcomes, and overall bias. Consensus was used to resolve any disagreements.

sec.title: 2.6. Statistical analysis
sec.p: Review Manager 5.4 was utilized to perform the meta-analysis. While we estimated the mean difference and the 95% CI for continuous data, we used the pooled relative risk (RR) with its 95% confidence interval (CI) for the analysis of dichotomous data. Statistical significance was defined as a P value of < .05. The statistic I2 was used to calculate the statistical heterogeneity between studies. When P < .1 or I2 > 50% were used to identify considerable heterogeneity, the random-effects model was applied; otherwise, the fixed-effects model was applied.

sec.title: 3.1. Search results
sec.p: Our database search yielded 652 articles in total, including 145 in PubMed, 208 in Web of Science, 240 in Embase, and 59 in the Cochrane Library. After getting rid of 220 duplicates and another 423 records by looking at the title and abstract, there were only 9 full-text publications left. Of these, 3 studies were eliminated because they involved non-RCTs. Six trials in total were included.[17–22] The workflow for literature screening is depicted in Figure 1.

caption.p: The flow diagram of study selection process.

sec.title: 3.2. Baseline characteristics of included studies
sec.p: The baseline characteristics of the included studies are shown in Table 1. The 6 included trials were all RCTs, and 3 of the study countries were Iran, 2 were Italy, and 1 was Spain. The maximum number of trial participants was 677, and the minimum was 71. The trials all compared the clinical effectiveness of methylprednisolone versus dexamethasone in the treatment of COVID-19.

sec.title: 3.3. Risk of bias
sec.p: The evaluation of the bias risk was demonstrated in Figures 2 and 3. As indicated, 2 open-label RCTs[17,20] were judged to have a high risk of the randomization process because both the trialists and subjects were aware of the intervention prior to grouping, and the remaining trials were low risk on all 5 evaluations. In addition, the 6 RCTs included were all rated low risk overall.

caption.p: Assessment of risk of bias for the studies.
Assessment of risk of bias for the studies.

sec.title: 3.4. Primary outcome
sec.p: All 6 trials reported data on all-cause mortality. In the methylprednisolone group of 704 patients, there were 77 fatalities (10.9%), while in the dexamethasone group of 699 patients, there were 92 fatalities (13.1%). There was no significant difference in mortality with MP compared with DXM (RR = 0.83, 95% CI [0.62, 1.10], P = .19, I2 = 0%) (Fig. 4). We found 2 trials[17,21] in which methylprednisolone was administered as a high-dose short-term pulse therapy (daily dose ≥250 mg for 3 days). We divided methylprednisolone into a high-dose group (RR = 0.85, 95% CI [0.47, 1.55], P = .59, I2 = 0%) and a low-dose group (RR = 0.82, 95% CI [0.60, 1.13], P = .23, I2 = 28%) for subgroup analysis, and we found no significant difference in mortality in either group compared with the control group (Fig. 5). The results of the Meta-analysis have been subjected to sensitivity analysis in Supplemental Digital Content (Fig. S1, http://links.lww.com/MD/J501), and the results indicate that the test results are reliable.

caption.p: Forest plots comparing methylprednisolone (MP) and dexamethasone (DXM) in coronavirus pandemic disease 2019 (COVID-19) regarding mortality.
Subgroup analysis for all-cause mortality according to the methylprednisolone (MP) dosage.

sec.title: 3.5. Secondary outcomes
sec.p: Five studies[17–19,21,22] compared the length of hospital stay for methylprednisolone versus dexamethasone for COVID-19; a meta-analysis showed no significant difference in the length of stay (mean difference = 0.31, 95% CI [−2.24, 2.85], P = .81, I2 = 95%) (Fig. 6). In the 5 studies,[17,18,20–22] there was no significant difference in ICU admissions between the MP group and the DXM group. (RR = 1.17, 95% CI [0.91, 1.50], P = .22, I2 = 0%) (Fig. 7). In the 4 trials,[17,19,20,22] there was no discernible difference in invasive mechanical ventilation between the MP group and the DXM group (RR = 0.84, 95% CI [0.54, 1.30], P = .43, I2 = 25%) (Fig. 8).

caption.p: Forest plots comparing methylprednisolone (MP) and dexamethasone (DXM) in coronavirus pandemic disease 2019 (COVID-19) regarding length of hospital stay.
Forest plots comparing methylprednisolone (MP) and dexamethasone (DXM) in coronavirus pandemic disease 2019 (COVID-19) regarding ICU admission.
Forest plots comparing methylprednisolone (MP) and dexamethasone (DXM) in coronavirus pandemic disease 2019 (COVID-19) regarding need for mechanical ventilation.

sec.p: In the results of 2 trials,[20,21] there was no statistically significant difference in the overall adverse events in the methylprednisolone group compared with the dexamethasone group in patients with neocoronary pneumonia (RR = 1.14, 95% CI [0.98, 1.34], P = .10, I2 = 0%) (Fig. 9), but in 3 trials,[17,18,20] it was mentioned that the incidence of hyperglycemia among the adverse events was higher in the methylprednisolone group than in the dexamethasone group (RR = 1.78, 95% CI [1.09, 2.89], P = .02, I2 = 78%) (Fig. 10). The above meta-analysis results were subjected to sensitivity analysis in Supplemental Digital Content (Figs. S2, S3, S4, and S5, http://links.lww.com/MD/J502).

caption.p: Forest plots comparing methylprednisolone (MP) and dexamethasone (DXM) in coronavirus pandemic disease 2019 (COVID-19) regarding overall adverse events.
Forest plots comparing methylprednisolone (MP) and dexamethasone (DXM) in coronavirus pandemic disease 2019 (COVID-19) regarding hyperglycemia.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: COVID-19 is a viral disease that is spreading quickly around the world, and scientists are working hard to find ways to treat it.[23] Respiratory or multi-organ failure caused by COVID-19 may be the result of an overactive immunological response that destroys pulmonary alveoli, resulting in severe cytokine and chemokine storms with systemic repercussions.[24] A lot of attention has been paid to how glucocorticoids help with inflammation and ARDS, and the hormones methylprednisolone and dexamethasone, which are usually used to treat diseases of the immune system and inflammation, have become one of the most important treatments in the COVID-19 epidemic.[8,25]

Which was more beneficial for COVID-19, methylprednisolone or dexamethasone? How should we choose when treating COVID-19? The current research was controversial. Some trials had compared MP to DXM in the treatment of COVID-19, and contradictory data had been found about the advantage of 1 steroid over the other.[26,27] For example, an RCT with 143 participants conducted by Dastenae et al[18] showed that dexamethasone 8 mg/day had better efficacy and a shorter length of stay than methylprednisolone 60 mg/day. However, the experiments studied by Saeed et al[12] suggested that methylprednisolone was superior to dexamethasone in the efficacy of COVID-19. In contrast, recent RCTs have shown no significant difference in the efficacy of methylprednisolone compared with dexamethasone in COVID-19.[28,29] The reasons for the inconsistent study results may include: the design method of the experiment; the number and type of cases included; the dosage and duration of the hormone; etc. There were also inconsistent results in the related meta-analysis. A meta-analysis of 6 studies[30] showed no difference between methylprednisolone and dexamethasone in terms of mortality or intubation requirements. Another meta-analysis of 3 RCTs[31] showed a substantially lower mortality rate for methylprednisolone compared with dexamethasone. However, the limitations of both analyses prevented the authors from reaching definitive conclusions. The problem with both analyses was that most of their results came from observational and nonrandomized studies, and only 3 RCTs were included.

We did a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs exclusively to increase the level of evidence and assess the efficacy and safety of methylprednisolone and dexamethasone in patients with COVID-19, given the uncertainty of the data from prior research and meta-analyses on this topic. Our study has significant advantages. First, we included only RCTs because they are more suitable for causal inference than observational studies. Then, all studies in our analysis were based on quality assessment with low risk of bias. This was a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs[17–22] with 1403 COVID-19 patients. All 6 RCTs included in the study showed no significant difference in mortality when comparing methylprednisolone with dexamethasone in the treatment of patients with COVID-19. Two of the trials[17,21] used methylprednisolone high-dose pulse therapy, and we performed subgroup analyses that did not yield differential results. Five RCTs[17–19,21,22] looked at length of stay. One trial[18] found that dexamethasone had a shorter length of stay than methylprednisolone, while another trial found the opposite. After our meta-analysis, we found that the difference was not statistically significant. The need for referral to the ICU was mentioned in 5 RCTs,[17,18,20–22] and none of the methylprednisolone groups were significantly different compared with the dexamethasone group. Overall adverse events were counted in 2 RCTs,[20,21] suggesting no statistical difference between the 2 groups, but in the 3 RCTs[17,18,20] involving hyperglycemia among adverse events, the incidence of hyperglycemia was higher with methylprednisolone than with dexamethasone, and the difference was statistically significant. Based on the results of our meta-analysis, there is currently no evidence as to whether methylprednisolone or dexamethasone is preferred for the treatment of COVID-19. We cautiously recommend that dexamethasone be considered a priority for patients with COVID-19 who are prone to hyperglycemic risk, such as those with combined diabetes.

Based on our findings, there was no significant difference in efficacy between methylprednisolone and dexamethasone in the treatment of COVID-9, and both had similar side effects. In general, the price of dexamethasone is relatively low compared to methylprednisolone, and dexamethasone may have an advantage in terms of cost-effectiveness. However, the exact choice of drug needs to be evaluated on the basis of the patient specific condition, the doctor recommendation, and the availability of the drug, taking into account other factors such as the patient history of drug allergies and contraindications. Therefore, when choosing a medication, one should look for one that meets the patient needs within a reasonable range.

With advances in genomics and biology, future research may focus more on individualized treatment. By analyzing a patient genotype and phenotype, it is possible to predict a patient response and tolerance to drugs, leading to a better selection of appropriate drugs and treatment regimens.

Our meta-analysis has several limitations. First, none of the 6 RCTs compared subgroups of critically ill COVID-19 patients requiring mechanical ventilation, and further studies are needed to determine whether methylprednisolone has a lower mortality rate than dexamethasone in this group of patients. Secondly, the RCTs included in this meta-analysis were mostly performed in Iran and Italy. Whether similar results have been found in other regions of the world needs to be confirmed by more studies. Third, these trials only included adults, so the impact on children is unknown.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: Based on the results of our meta-analysis, there is no evidence to suggest that methylprednisolone or dexamethasone is superior for treating COVID-19. Nevertheless, methylprednisolone may be more likely to cause hyperglycemia than dexamethasone.
